title: The Importance of Being Earnest
author: Oscar Wilde
setting: A flat in Half-Moon Street, Mayfair, and the garden and drawing room of a manor house at Woolton, Hertfordshire
lengthNote: Three acts of continuous prose dialogue, reduced by Wilde from an earlier four-act version
openingLine: Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?
summary: Two young men have each invented a person who does not exist in order to get out of obligations, and both find themselves engaged to women who will only marry a man called Ernest. Wilde builds a farce in which the plot is entirely conventional and the sentences are not: every line of feeling arrives inverted, and the discovery that resolves everything is produced out of a hand-bag left in a railway cloakroom.
referenceStyle: act. The play is continuous prose dialogue and the text checked against carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by act and by the point in the action they belong to.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Importance of Being Earnest
sourceText.note: The three-act text, following the first book edition of 1899. Because it is prose without line numbering, references give the act alone.

atAGlance.label: First performed
atAGlance.note: At the St James's Theatre, London, managed by George Alexander, who played Jack.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Published by Leonard Smithers; the title page names the author through Lady Windermere's Fan rather than printing his name.

atAGlance.label: Subtitle
atAGlance.value: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People
atAGlance.note: The joke is the arrangement: triviality is the discipline, seriousness the affliction.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Cut down from a four-act draft, which removed an entire subplot about a solicitor come to arrest Ernest for unpaid dinners.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Half-Moon Street: a cigarette case and an interview
structure.summary: Algernon produces an inscribed cigarette case and forces Jack to confess that he is Jack in the country and Ernest in town. Gwendolen accepts a proposal on the strength of a name, and her mother interviews the candidate, finds his origins to be a railway cloakroom, and refuses.

scenes.summary: Lane and the cucumber sandwiches; Algernon extracts the truth about Cecily and the double life.
Jack's imaginary brother is matched against Algernon's imaginary invalid.
Gwendolen announces that her ideal has always been to love a man called Ernest, and Jack proposes on his knees.
Lady Bracknell's examination of income, politics, property and parentage ends at the hand-bag.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The garden at Woolton: two Ernests at once
structure.summary: Algernon arrives in the country as the wicked brother and is engaged to Cecily inside half an hour, having been engaged to her in her diary for months already. Jack comes home in mourning for a brother who is standing on the lawn, and the two women meet over tea and discover they are engaged to the same name.

scenes.summary: Miss Prism, Dr Chasuble and a chapter on the Fall of the Rupee that may be omitted.
Algernon presents himself as Jack's brother and Cecily produces the record of their engagement.
Jack returns in black to announce a death that contradicts the guest in the garden.
Gwendolen and Cecily compare diaries, sugar and cake, and conclude they have both been deceived.
Both men book the same clergyman for the same afternoon and the same name.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The drawing room: a hand-bag, and a christening cancelled
structure.summary: Lady Bracknell arrives, approves of Cecily's money and forbids Algernon's engagement until Jack forbids Cecily's, at which point Miss Prism is recognised, the hand-bag is produced and Jack turns out to be Algernon's elder brother. His father's name is looked up in an Army List and is, inevitably, Ernest.

scenes.summary: Lady Bracknell's objections to Cecily evaporate on hearing the figure in the Funds.
Jack refuses consent for Cecily until his own engagement is allowed.
A governess, a perambulator, a three-volume novel and a hand-bag left at Victoria Station.
Jack's real name is found in print, and the title of the play is spoken as its last line.

characters.name: John Worthing, J.P.
characters.role: A country landowner and magistrate, Cecily's guardian
characters.summary: He maintains a wicked younger brother in town so that he can be respectable in Hertfordshire, and takes the high moral tone in the country because he has invented somewhere else to be immoral. He is the only character who wants a settled identity, and the plot hands him one he has been using by accident for years.
characters.clue: He was found in a hand-bag at a railway cloakroom, is a magistrate in one county and a scoundrel in another, and turns out to have been telling the truth all along.

relationships.label: friend of, and unknowingly brother to

characters.name: Algernon Moncrieff
characters.role: Lady Bracknell's nephew, of Half-Moon Street
characters.summary: He eats continuously, owes money everywhere, and has invented a permanently ill friend whose relapses can be timed to avoid any dinner he does not want. He is the play's theorist, supplying most of its paradoxes, and the only person in it who is entirely unembarrassed by his own behaviour.
characters.clue: He keeps an invalid friend whose health fails precisely when a family dinner is proposed, and eats every muffin in the dish while a crisis is going on.

relationships.label: friend and, it emerges, brother of

characters.name: Hon. Gwendolen Fairfax
characters.summary: She speaks in her mother's cadences about entirely different things, and she has settled the question of whom she will marry before meeting anyone: it must be a man called Ernest. Her certainty is unshakeable and her reasoning is decorative, which makes her a comic character and also, in the tea scene, a formidable one.
characters.clue: She will only marry a man with one particular name, and travels with a diary so that she always has something sensational to read.

characters.name: Cecily Cardew
characters.role: Jack's ward, at the Manor House
characters.summary: She has been conducting an engagement to a man she has never met for three months in a diary, including the letters he wrote her and the week they were broken off. Wilde gives the country ingenue the most thoroughly fictional inner life in the play, and it is entirely in writing.
characters.clue: She waters roses to avoid German grammar and has already recorded, in her diary, the proposal she is about to receive.

characters.name: Lady Bracknell
characters.summary: She conducts marriage as a matter of lists, incomes and addresses, and delivers her most outrageous positions in the tone of settled common sense. She was herself without fortune when she married, which she mentions once, and that single admission is the crack in an otherwise seamless piece of masonry.
characters.clue: She keeps a list of eligible young men, disapproves of education on the grounds that ignorance is a delicate fruit, and changes her mind about a girl the moment she hears the figure.

characters.name: Miss Prism
characters.summary: She wrote a three-volume novel of more than usually revolting sentimentality, mislaid it in a perambulator and deposited the baby in a hand-bag at Victoria Station. The play's entire machinery of discovery rests on a woman who has spent two acts recommending moral fiction and disapproving of everybody.
characters.clue: She once put a manuscript where a baby should have been, and has been giving German lessons ever since.

characters.name: Rev. Canon Chasuble, D.D.
characters.summary: He has a sermon adaptable to almost any occasion, joyful or distressing, and is prepared to christen two grown men in one afternoon. His courtship of Miss Prism proceeds entirely in metaphors about bees and education, and neither party ever says anything directly until the last minute of the play.
characters.clue: He has one sermon he has preached at harvest celebrations, christenings, confirmations and days of humiliation, and is prepared to baptise two grown men in one afternoon.

characters.name: Lane
characters.summary: He drinks the champagne, keeps the accounts of the cucumber sandwiches and declines to have opinions in a way that is itself an opinion. His handful of lines are placed where they will deflate his employer's, and they do it without ever ceasing to be perfectly correct.
characters.clue: He did not think it polite to listen to the piano, and explains that in married households the champagne is rarely of a first-rate brand.

themes.name: Earnestness and triviality
themes.summary: The play takes the highest Victorian virtue and reduces it to a name that can be acquired at a christening for half a crown. Nobody in it is sincere and nobody suffers for that; the characters who talk most about duty, morality and improving literature are the ones caught out, and the ones who admit to inventing their lives get what they want.
themes.development: Jack adopts a high moral tone in Act I because he has somewhere else to misbehave; by the last line the word earnest has been converted into a proper noun and a joke.

themes.name: Names and identity
themes.summary: Two women will marry a name rather than a man, and two men undertake to be rechristened to supply it. Jack's search for his parents is, in the end, a search for an entry in a printed list, and the play's happy ending consists of a fact being looked up in the Army Lists rather than felt.
themes.development: A name invented in Act I, promised to two women in Act II, and finally discovered to have been legally correct from the start in Act III.

themes.name: Marriage as a transaction
themes.summary: Lady Bracknell conducts courtship as due diligence: income, investments, town address, politics, parentage. Wilde's joke is not that she is wrong about how it works but that she says so out loud, and her objections to Cecily disappear the instant a number is mentioned.
themes.development: A list of eligible young men in Act I, a valuation of a Hertfordshire estate, and an about-turn in Act III on the strength of a figure in the Funds.

themes.name: Town and country, and the double life
themes.summary: Bunburying is the play's word for the arrangement that lets a respectable life continue: a place where one is not, and a person one is not, held in reserve. The comedy's geography is moral, and the two halves have to be kept from meeting, which is exactly what Act II arranges.
themes.development: Two invented people in Act I, both physically present in Act II, and both killed off before the christenings can be booked.

themes.name: Diaries, letters and the written record
themes.summary: Nearly every fact in the play is documented before it happens. Cecily's engagement exists in her diary, Gwendolen carries hers for the sensational reading, Miss Prism's novel is lost in a perambulator and Jack's name is confirmed by the Army Lists. Writing here does not record events; it creates them.
themes.development: An inscription inside a cigarette case in Act I, two diaries in conflict in Act II, and a shelf of Army Lists settling the plot in Act III.

themes.name: Servants, food and appetite
themes.summary: Cucumber sandwiches, bread and butter, muffins, tea and sugar are the currency of every quarrel, and the servants keep the accounts. Emotional crises in this play are conducted over plates, and Wilde uses eating as the only honest appetite anybody displays.
themes.development: Sandwiches ordered for an aunt and eaten before she arrives in Act I, sugar and cake used as weapons in Act II, and muffins consumed during the collapse of both engagements.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short, polished statement that sounds like settled wisdom.
techniques.inThisBook: Wilde gives the epigrams to the characters least entitled to them, so that a manservant, an idler and a snob all speak with the authority of a proverb.

techniques.name: Inversion
techniques.definition: Reversing a received sentiment so that the expected term ends up in the wrong place.
techniques.inThisBook: Divorces made in heaven, three being company in marriage, style mattering more than sincerity: the form is always a maxim and the content is always its opposite.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A sentence that descends abruptly from the elevated to the trivial.
techniques.inThisBook: Lady Bracknell moves from the excesses of the French Revolution to a cloakroom at a railway station, and the drop is the joke.

techniques.name: Farce structure
techniques.definition: Symmetrical plotting in which two of everything collide.
techniques.inThisBook: Two invented people, two men called Ernest, two engagements, two christenings booked with one clergyman for the same afternoon, and one hand-bag to undo it all.

techniques.name: The stage property
techniques.definition: An object that carries the plot rather than decorating it.
techniques.inThisBook: The inscribed cigarette case exposes Jack, the diaries authorise both engagements, and the hand-bag delivers the recognition scene.

techniques.name: The deflating servant
techniques.definition: A subordinate whose brief, correct replies undercut the speaker above them.
techniques.inThisBook: Lane's refusal to have listened to the piano, and his account of married households and champagne, set the play's tone before Jack has entered.

quotations.text: I didn’t think it polite to listen, sir.
quotations.speaker: Lane
quotations.context: Answering Algernon's question about the piano, in the play's fourth line.
quotations.analysis: The servant declines to have heard something everyone in the theatre has just heard, and does it by appealing to manners rather than to fact. Within four lines Wilde has established the rule the whole play runs on: politeness is a technique for not knowing things.

quotations.text: The truth is rarely pure and never simple.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Pressing Jack to admit that Cecily exists.
quotations.analysis: The line is an epigram in defence of an interrogation, which is a peculiar use for it. Wilde puts the play's most quotable statement about truth in the mouth of the man currently telling the fewest lies, and follows it immediately with a joke about modern literature.

quotations.text: Divorces are made in Heaven
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: On marriage, moments before defending the cucumber sandwiches.
quotations.analysis: One word is swapped in a proverb and the sentiment is reversed without a syllable of argument. The line is also interrupted mid-breath by Algernon stopping Jack taking a sandwich, so that the epigram and the appetite share a sentence.

quotations.text: You have invented a very useful younger brother called Ernest, in order that you may be able to come up to town as often as you like. I have invented an invaluable permanent invalid called Bunbury, in order that I may be able to go down into the country whenever I choose.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Naming Jack's deception and matching it with his own.
quotations.analysis: The two fictions are laid out in parallel clauses, and the symmetry is the play's architecture in advance: town and country, brother and invalid, each man needing somewhere he is not. Note that both inventions are described as useful, which is the only virtue either man claims for them.

quotations.text: You don’t seem to realise, that in married life three is company and two is none.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Warning Jack that a married man will need Bunbury.
quotations.analysis: Two is company, three is none goes in and comes out reversed, so that adultery is described in the vocabulary of good manners. It is also a plot prediction: by Act II there are indeed three people in each engagement, and one of them does not exist.

quotations.text: I hate people who are not serious about meals. It is so shallow of them.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Interrupting a discussion of the evening's arrangements.
quotations.analysis: Seriousness, the quality the whole play is named for, is transferred to dinner, and shallowness becomes a charge against people who are not hungry. The joke works because Algernon means it entirely: his appetite is the one sincere thing in the comedy.

quotations.text: The fact is constantly mentioned in the more expensive monthly magazines, and has reached the provincial pulpits, I am told; and my ideal has always been to love someone of the name of Ernest. There is something in that name that inspires absolute confidence.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Explaining to Jack, before he has proposed, why she has decided to love him.
quotations.analysis: Her ideal is not a man but a set of syllables, and she supports it with the monthly magazines and the provincial pulpits, as though it were a matter of public opinion. Everything Jack has invented to make himself free has turned out to be the one condition he cannot meet.

quotations.text: To lose one parent, Mr. Worthing, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: During the interview, on learning that Jack has lost both his parents.
quotations.analysis: Bereavement is reclassified as a lapse of organisation, and the balance of the sentence, misfortune against carelessness, does the reclassifying without an argument. It is the clearest example in the play of Wilde giving a monstrous position the rhythm of common sense.

quotations.text: A handbag?
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: On being told where Jack was found as a baby.
quotations.analysis: Two words, and they are the most famous in the English comic theatre because the actor has to decide the entire character on them. The line is a question that is not asking for information; it is a whole social order failing to accommodate a piece of luggage.

quotations.text: I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: On being told that Jack knows nothing.
quotations.analysis: Ignorance is given the vocabulary of horticulture and the protection usually reserved for virtue. The sentence that follows extends the compliment to English education on the grounds that it produces no effect whatsoever, which is Wilde attacking his own class from inside its drawing room.

quotations.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: Assessing Jack's Hertfordshire estate during the interview.
quotations.analysis: This is the play's one piece of genuine economics, spoken by its least reflective character: agricultural land in the 1890s really had stopped paying, and estates really were maintained for the position they conferred. The joke is that she states the whole agricultural depression as a social inconvenience.

quotations.text: Cecily, you will read your Political Economy in my absence. The chapter on the Fall of the Rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.
quotations.speaker: Miss Prism
quotations.context: Leaving Cecily to her lessons while she walks with Dr Chasuble.
quotations.analysis: The collapse of the rupee had ruined real fortunes and salaries across the Empire, which is precisely why it is too sensational for a schoolroom. Wilde's governess protects her pupil from the one subject in the curriculum that describes the world she actually lives in.

quotations.text: The good ended happily, and the bad unhappily. That is what Fiction means.
quotations.speaker: Miss Prism
quotations.context: Describing the three-volume novel she once wrote.
quotations.analysis: A whole theory of the improving Victorian novel in fourteen words, delivered by the woman whose own carelessness with a perambulator will supply this play's ending. The capital letter on Fiction is doing the work: she is defining a genre, not describing a book.

quotations.text: I hope you have not been leading a double life, pretending to be wicked and being really good all the time. That would be hypocrisy.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: To Algernon, who is at that moment leading a double life in the other direction.
quotations.analysis: Hypocrisy is redefined as the pretence of wickedness, which inverts the standard Victorian charge exactly. Cecily is right about the double life and wrong about which way round it runs, and the audience is the only party in the garden that knows both halves.

quotations.text: You must not laugh at me, darling, but it had always been a girlish dream of mine to love someone whose name was Ernest.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: Accepting Algernon while explaining the condition she has always attached.
quotations.analysis: The second woman arrives at the identical requirement independently, and Wilde makes no attempt to explain the coincidence because the play is not interested in psychology. The effect is to turn a private preference into something more like a law of nature.

quotations.text: I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read in the train.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Producing documentary evidence during the tea-table confrontation with Cecily.
quotations.analysis: The diary is introduced as proof and described as entertainment in consecutive sentences, which tells the audience exactly how much the evidence is worth. Both women are now arguing from written records of events that never happened.

quotations.text: This is no time for wearing the shallow mask of manners. When I see a spade I call it a spade.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: At the height of the tea-table quarrel with Gwendolen.
quotations.analysis: The country girl claims plain speaking as a virtue, in a sentence that is itself a cliche about not using cliches. Gwendolen's reply, that she is glad to say she has never seen a spade, turns the claim into a statement about class within two lines.

quotations.text: I am glad to say that I have never seen a spade. It is obvious that our social spheres have been widely different.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Answering Cecily, marked in the text as spoken satirically.
quotations.analysis: She takes a dead metaphor completely literally and converts it into evidence of rank, which is the fastest piece of social violence in the play. The second sentence is delivered as a neutral observation, and that flatness is what makes it cut.

quotations.text: In matters of grave importance, style, not sincerity is the vital thing.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Agreeing with Cecily on how to receive the men's explanations.
quotations.analysis: This is the play's own defence, stated by a character as a rule of etiquette. It also inverts the usual hierarchy under which sincerity excuses a clumsy apology, and it arrives just before both women accept explanations they know to be worthless.

quotations.text: Never speak disrespectfully of Society, Algernon. Only people who can’t get into it do that.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: Rebuking her nephew during the negotiation over Cecily.
quotations.analysis: The defence of Society is conducted entirely by sneering at outsiders, which concedes the criticism while appearing to refuse it. Wilde, who was about to be put outside it himself, gives the line to the character with the most to lose from anyone examining the claim.

quotations.text: On the contrary, Aunt Augusta, I’ve now realised for the first time in my life the vital Importance of Being Earnest.
quotations.speaker: Jack
quotations.context: The last line of the play, answering the charge that he has been trivial.
quotations.analysis: The title arrives as a pun that has taken three acts to load: the quality and the name have become the same word, and the discovery that resolves everything is a matter of spelling. Wilde ends a comedy about sincerity by proving that the hero was accurate all along, and entirely by accident.

timeline.label: Oscar Wilde born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford.

timeline.label: The Picture of Dorian Gray published in book form
timeline.detail: Expanded from the magazine version of the previous year, with a preface answering its critics.

timeline.label: Lady Windermere's Fan opens at the St James's Theatre
timeline.detail: The first of the society comedies, and the play the title page of the 1899 Earnest uses to identify its author.

timeline.label: A Woman of No Importance opens
timeline.detail: The second society comedy, at the Haymarket.

timeline.label: Earnest written, largely at Worthing
timeline.detail: Wilde took a house on the Sussex coast with his family for the late summer; the hero's surname comes from the town.

timeline.label: An Ideal Husband opens in January
timeline.detail: For a few weeks in early 1895 Wilde had two plays running in the West End at once.

timeline.label: First performance, 14 February
timeline.detail: At the St James's Theatre, with George Alexander as Jack; the run ended within months when Wilde was tried and imprisoned.

timeline.label: Wilde released from Reading Gaol
timeline.detail: He left England for France and never returned.

timeline.label: First book edition, Leonard Smithers
timeline.detail: The three-act text corrected by Wilde, in a small issue of numbered and signed copies.

timeline.label: Wilde dies in Paris
timeline.detail: Three years after his release, and before the play had returned to the London stage under his name.

timeline.label: Anthony Asquith's film released
timeline.detail: With Edith Evans as Lady Bracknell, whose reading of the hand-bag line has shaped every performance since.

places.name: Half-Moon Street, Mayfair
places.note: Algernon's flat, and the setting of the whole first act.

places.name: St James's Theatre, King Street
places.note: Where the play opened on 14 February 1895 under George Alexander's management; the building was demolished in 1957.

places.name: Victoria Station
places.note: The cloakroom where the hand-bag was deposited, on the Brighton line.

places.name: Worthing, West Sussex
places.note: Where Wilde wrote the play in the late summer of 1894, and where the hero got his surname.

places.name: Dublin
places.note: Wilde's birthplace and the city of his education before Oxford.

criticalViews.position: A perfect farce and nothing more
criticalViews.summary: The oldest account, and Wilde's own framing in the subtitle: a comedy whose subject is its own construction, where the plotting is symmetrical, the dialogue is polished and the pleasure is entirely formal.
criticalViews.counter: It has to ignore how much of the laughter comes from money, rank and the machinery of a marriage market that the play describes with considerable accuracy.

criticalViews.position: A comedy about the double life
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the middle of the twentieth century has read Bunburying as a figure for lives lived in two places at once, written months before Wilde's own prosecution made the arrangement a matter of public record.
criticalViews.counter: Read too directly, it turns a play whose whole method is surface into a coded confession, which is the one thing its style refuses to be.

criticalViews.position: A satire of the late-Victorian ruling class
criticalViews.summary: Lady Bracknell's interview, the agricultural depression, the Funds, the London season and the servants' commentary place the comedy precisely in a class whose income and confidence were both under pressure in the 1890s.
criticalViews.counter: The satire is affectionate enough to be enjoyed by its targets, and the play ends by rewarding everyone in it with money and a title.

essayQuestions.question: How does Wilde use the idea of earnestness in the play?
essayQuestions.focus: The title, the name and the Victorian virtue
plan: Separate the two senses at once: the moral quality and the proper noun, and show how the play keeps them colliding.
Use Jack's high moral tone in Act I, adopted precisely so that he can misbehave elsewhere.
Examine the two women's requirement that a husband be called Ernest, and the fact that neither offers a reason.
Set the christenings against the discovery in the Army Lists: one is a decision, the other a fact.
Close on the last line and decide what Wilde has proved about sincerity by making it a question of spelling.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Lady Bracknell's function in the comedy.
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, money and the sound of common sense
plan: Analyse the interview in Act I as a procedure: income, investments, address, politics, parentage, in that order.
Show how Wilde gives outrageous positions the cadence of settled wisdom, using the lines on ignorance and on land.
Note the single admission that she married without a fortune, and what it does to her authority.
Track the reversal in Act III when Cecily's money is mentioned, and how quickly the objections dissolve.
Assess whether she is a satirical target, a comic engine, or the only character who tells the truth about the system.

essayQuestions.question: What part do written documents play in the plot?
plan: Start with the cigarette case, whose inscription begins the exposure of Jack's arrangement.
Compare Cecily's diary, which records an engagement that has not happened, with Gwendolen's, which is carried for entertainment.
Consider Miss Prism's three-volume novel and the perambulator, the play's most consequential piece of writing.
Examine the Army Lists as the instrument of resolution, and what it means that a fact is settled by looking it up.
Conclude on the pattern: in this play writing does not record events, it authorises them.

essayQuestions.question: 'A play in which nobody is sincere and nobody suffers for it.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Morality, consequence and the shape of the ending
plan: List the deceptions in play by the end of Act II and note that none of them is punished.
Contrast the characters who preach improvement, Miss Prism and Chasuble, with those who admit to invention.
Test the statement against Lady Bracknell, who is never deceived and never apologises for anything.
Weigh the ending: two marriages, a fortune, a brother and a name, all delivered by coincidence.
Decide whether the absence of consequence is a moral evasion or the precise point of the form.

discussionQuestions: Both women insist on marrying a man called Ernest, and neither will say why. Does the play want us to find a reason?
Algernon eats through every crisis in the play. What does his appetite do that his epigrams cannot?
Lady Bracknell says the most outrageous things in the calmest voice. Is she a monster, or simply the only character stating the terms out loud?
The plot is resolved by a hand-bag and a shelf of Army Lists. Is that a weakness in the play or the whole joke?
Lane speaks about a dozen lines. Why does Wilde open the play with him rather than with Algernon?

related.why: Wilde's novel of the same decade, with the same epigrams put to an entirely unfunny purpose.
The comic ancestor: two couples, a wit who will not admit to feeling, and a plot driven by what people are told rather than what is true.
The other great English comedy of income, property and a formidable older woman investigating a marriage.
Assumed identities, mistaken names and a resolution that arrives when two people who look alike are finally in the same room.
The same 1890s society viewed from several rungs down, and also told through a diary that its keeper takes very seriously.
